client: I've been really struggling lately with this overwhelming dread about my final exams coming up next month. After how badly last term went for me, I just keep thinking there's no way I can turn things around in time. Honestly, I'm not even sure talking about it is going to change anything, but I figured I'd try.
therapist: It means a lot that you reached out even when part of you felt uncertain it would help — that took real courage, and I'm glad you're here. It sounds like last term left a painful mark, and your mind is now using that experience as "evidence" that the same outcome is inevitable, which makes the dread feel so heavy and real. I'm curious — when you imagine the worst happening with your exams, what's the specific thought or fear that tends to feel loudest for you?

client: I guess the loudest thought is something like... "you're going to blank out completely and everyone will see how stupid you actually are." It's not just about failing the exam itself, it's more like this fear that it'll prove something that I already secretly believe about myself. And once that thought shows up, it kind of takes over everything and I can't really think straight anymore.
therapist: That thought — "this will prove I'm actually stupid" — is such a painful one to carry, and it makes complete sense that it hijacks your thinking, because it feels like so much more than an exam is on the line. I'd gently invite you to notice that this is a belief about yourself, not a fact, and beliefs formed in hard moments don't always tell the whole truth. What evidence have you seen in your life — even small moments — that might not fit with the idea that you're "actually stupid"?

client: I hear what you're saying, and I guess... there have been moments. Like, I did really well in my history class last semester, and my professor actually asked me to share my essay with the rest of the group. But when I try to hold onto that right now, it just feels far away, like it doesn't count the same way this exam does, and I'm not sure why I can't let it actually mean something.
therapist: That memory of your professor highlighting your essay is genuinely meaningful evidence, and the fact that you could recall it matters — even if it feels distant right now. What's happening is really common in CBT: when we're in the grip of a strong negative belief, our mind tends to "discount" the contradicting evidence, almost like it moves the goalposts to protect the belief from being challenged. I wonder — what do you think would need to be true for that history success to feel like it "counts" just as much as this exam does?

client: I guess... for it to really count, I'd have to believe that one good thing wasn't just a fluke, you know? Like, my brain keeps telling me that the professor was probably just being nice, or that essay was a easier assignment, so it doesn't really prove anything about whether I can handle hard stuff like this exam. It's frustrating because I can see what you're describing — that goalpost-moving thing — but even knowing that's happening doesn't make it stop.
therapist: You've just done something really insightful — you caught your mind generating "yes, but" explanations in real time, which is actually a sophisticated skill, even if it doesn't feel like one right now. You're right that awareness alone doesn't automatically silence the thought, but it does create a tiny bit of space between you and it, and that space is where change begins to grow. I'm curious — if a close friend came to you with exactly the same history essay success and the same upcoming exam fear, would you so quickly tell them it was probably just a fluke?

client: Honestly, no, I wouldn't tell a friend it was a fluke — I'd probably point out everything they did right and tell them they should feel proud. But it feels different when it's me, like the rules just don't apply the same way, and I know that sounds contradictory but I can't help it. I guess I'm just not sure how to make myself believe what I'd easily tell someone else.
therapist: What you just noticed — that you hold yourself to a harsher standard than you'd ever apply to someone you care about — is one of the most important insights in this kind of work, and the fact that it feels contradictory means you're already seeing it clearly. That gap between what we know intellectually and what we actually feel is real, and bridging it takes practice rather than just willpower or logic. I wonder if, over the next few days, you'd be willing to try a small experiment: when that "it doesn't count" thought shows up, gently ask yourself "what would I say to my friend here?" — not to force a feeling, but just to notice what happens when you borrow a little of that compassion for yourself?

client: I hear what you're saying, and part of me does want to try it. But honestly, my first reaction is that it feels a little artificial, like I'd just be going through the motions without actually believing it. I guess my worry is that asking "what would I say to a friend" will just remind me how far I am from actually feeling that way about myself, and that might make things worse instead of better.
therapist: That concern is really valid, and it actually shows a lot of self-awareness — forcing positivity that feels hollow can sometimes backfire, and it's wise that you're noticing that risk rather than just blindly trying things. What I'd gently offer is that the goal isn't to instantly *feel* the compassion, but simply to notice the contrast between the two voices, almost like a curious observer rather than someone trying to convince themselves of something. What do you think it would feel like to approach that exercise with curiosity rather than pressure — just watching what comes up, without needing it to fix anything right away?

client: I guess that sounds a little less threatening when you put it that way — like I don't have to force myself to feel something I don't. But I'm still not sure I trust myself to be a "curious observer" when I'm in the middle of beating myself up, because in those moments it feels like the critical voice just takes over completely and there's no space for anything else. It's like trying to watch a storm from inside the storm.
therapist: "Trying to watch a storm from inside the storm" is a beautiful and honest description, and it tells me that in those intense moments, asking yourself to observe might genuinely be too big a leap — and that's okay, we don't have to start there. Sometimes it helps to practice the "curious observer" stance during calmer moments, almost like a rehearsal, so that it becomes a little more familiar before the storm hits. I'm wondering — are there quieter moments in your day, even brief ones, where the critical voice is a little less loud and you might have just a bit more breathing room to experiment?

client: I mean, yeah, sometimes in the morning before I've really started thinking about the day, there are a few minutes where it's quieter. But honestly, even then I feel this kind of low-level hum of dread, like I'm just waiting for the voice to start up again. I'm not sure if that counts as "breathing room" or if I'd just be practicing in a minefield.
therapist: Even a few quieter morning minutes absolutely counts — it doesn't need to be perfectly peaceful to be useful, just slightly less intense than the storm itself. That low-level hum you're describing is actually really important information, because it suggests your nervous system is working hard even at rest, bracing for something it's learned to expect. I'm curious — in those morning moments, what's the very first thing your mind tends to reach for, and do you think there's anything, however small, that makes those minutes feel even slightly safer than the rest of the day?

client: Honestly, the first thing my mind reaches for is my phone — I check my messages almost immediately, like I'm bracing to find out if someone's upset with me or if I missed something important. And I think that's actually what makes those minutes feel less safe, not more, because I'm basically inviting the anxiety in before I've even sat up properly. I know that probably sounds counterproductive, but it's like I'd rather know the bad news right away than lie there dreading it.
therapist: What you just described is such a clear and honest piece of self-awareness — you've identified that reaching for your phone is actually a way of trying to *control* the dread, even though it ends up feeding it rather than soothing it. That makes complete sense as a coping strategy, because uncertainty feels unbearable when you're already braced for something bad, and checking feels like it gives you back some control. I'm wondering — what do you imagine might happen in those morning minutes if you waited just a little longer before reaching for your phone, and what feels most scary about that idea?

client: Honestly, when I imagine just lying there without reaching for my phone, the first thing that comes up is this kind of... hollow, sinking feeling, like I'm just waiting for something bad to confirm itself. I think what scares me most is that without the checking, I have nothing to do with all that dread, and it just sits there getting bigger. At least when I'm scrolling or checking messages, I feel like I'm doing something, even if I know deep down it's not actually helping.
therapist: What you're describing - that the checking feels like *doing something* with unbearable feelings even when it doesn't truly help - is at the heart of how anxiety keeps itself alive, and recognizing that cycle so clearly is genuinely significant work. That hollow, sinking feeling you'd face without the phone isn't actually the dread getting bigger - it might just be the dread becoming more visible, which feels the same but is actually different. I'm curious - has there ever been a time in your life when you sat with an uncomfortable feeling without trying to escape it, and found that it eventually shifted on its own, even just a little?
